title: Supporting your Autistic child to flourish

segments.spoken_text:
Welcome to our Parents and Carers workshop, supporting your Autistic child to flourish. I'm glad you've made some time for this. You might be arriving with a clear question, or after a very full morning. Either way, you're welcome here.

Today we'll build on what you already know about your child, explore some shared language, and consider supports that fit your family. Keep your workbook nearby. In this walkthrough, activity pauses are brief. Whenever you need more time to think, write or talk, pause the video and resume when you're ready.
segments.source_note: Parents and Carers - Primary, Session 1, slide 1; matching slide PDF page 1; updated PPTX speaker notes (28 September 2026). Authored audience-facing delivery, with optional participation and no invented participant responses.

segments.spoken_text:
I acknowledge the Traditional Custodians of the lands on which we are learning today, and pay my respects to Elders past and present. I recognise the continuing connections of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples to Country, culture and community.

I extend that respect to Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people taking part in this learning today.
segments.source_note: Parents and Carers - Primary, Session 1, slide 2; matching slide PDF page 2; updated PPTX speaker notes (28 September 2026). Authored audience-facing delivery, with optional participation and no invented participant responses. Generic Acknowledgement reused from approved simulations; no unverified local Custodian name asserted.

segments.spoken_text: Our Statement of Reconciliation is in your workbook for you to read. For the sake of this demonstration, I'll read it aloud. We at Positive Partnerships value and recognise the diversity of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander cultures and heritage and their proud part in Australia’s national identity. We acknowledge and continue to learn about Australia’s colonial past and the historic and ongoing impacts on Australia’s First Nations people. We believe in and strongly support the Truth-telling of Australia’s colonial history and in moving forward as a nation we must encourage open, honest dialogue and build relationships built on respect and trust.
segments.source_note: Parents and Carers - Primary, Session 1, slide 3; matching slide PDF page 3; updated PPTX speaker notes (28 September 2026). PC Primary - Workbook PDF page 1. Authored audience-facing delivery, with optional participation and no invented participant responses. Exact user-supplied reconciliation statement with approved workbook/demonstration introduction; statement confirmed on Workbook page 1.

segments.spoken_text: First Nations people are advised that this workshop may contain images and voices of people who are no longer with us.
segments.source_note: Parents and Carers - Primary, Session 1, slide 4; matching slide PDF page 4; updated PPTX speaker notes (28 September 2026). Authored audience-facing delivery, with optional participation and no invented participant responses.

segments.spoken_text:
Everyone is welcome to be themselves here. You can move, stand, fidget, listen, write, step out or pass on an activity. Use whatever helps you take part. Some parents and carers here may be Autistic or otherwise neurodivergent themselves. Your experience is welcome too.

Your workbook belongs to you, and you decide what to share. Please keep other families' stories private. When we discuss school or family situations, leave out identifying details. We can learn from a situation while respecting the people involved.
segments.source_note: Parents and Carers - Primary, Session 1, slide 5; matching slide PDF page 5; updated PPTX speaker notes (28 September 2026). Authored audience-facing delivery, with optional participation and no invented participant responses.

segments.spoken_text:
Before we settle in, take a moment to check your surroundings: the exits, bathroom facilities, refreshments and any quiet space available. Follow the arrangements for your venue, including smoking and vaping. If you're watching elsewhere, make the space as comfortable as you can.

Keep your phone available if you need to be contacted by school or a carer, and be considerate about sounds and calls. Have your workbook and something to write with nearby. You can write questions down, and in a live workshop you can ask the delivery team privately or during a break. Attend to your own needs as we go.
segments.source_note: Parents and Carers - Primary, Session 1, slide 6; matching slide PDF page 6; updated PPTX speaker notes (28 September 2026). Authored audience-facing delivery, with optional participation and no invented participant responses.

segments.spoken_text:
Let's meet the people around us. At your table, share your first name and who you're here for. You might include your child's age or year level, if you'd like to. Then share one thing you would like to understand by the end of the day.

Keep it brief so everyone has room, and remember you can pass. There's no need to share a diagnosis, school name or private family circumstances. If you're watching on your own, make a note of your question on page four of the workbook. Pause here for your introductions.
segments.screen_cue: Allow 4 minutes for introductions. Pause the video, then resume for the debrief.
segments.source_note: Parents and Carers - Primary, Session 1, slide 7; matching slide PDF page 7; updated PPTX speaker notes (28 September 2026). PC Primary - Workbook PDF page 4. Authored audience-facing delivery, with optional participation and no invented participant responses.

segments.spoken_text: Let's come back. Write your one thing on page four if you haven't already. Keep that question with you. We'll return to it in our final session and consider what has become clearer, as well as what you'd still like to explore.
segments.source_note: Parents and Carers - Primary, Session 1, slide 7; matching slide PDF page 7; updated PPTX speaker notes (28 September 2026). PC Primary - Workbook PDF page 4. Authored audience-facing delivery, with optional participation and no invented participant responses.

segments.spoken_text:
Here's the shape of our day. We begin with your child as a whole person, then explore sensory experience and thinking. After morning tea, we move into communication, connection and daily capacity. The afternoon turns towards home and community, followed by partnership with school. Our final session brings the learning back to a few small next steps.

The timetable on the slide is a guide for a live workshop, including morning tea from eleven to eleven fifteen and lunch from twelve fifteen to twelve forty-five. In this recording, take breaks when you need them. These six sessions are connected, so keep the same child in mind throughout.
segments.source_note: Parents and Carers - Primary, Session 1, slide 8; matching slide PDF page 8; updated PPTX speaker notes (28 September 2026). Authored audience-facing delivery, with optional participation and no invented participant responses.

segments.spoken_text:
A quick word about language. You'll hear us say Autistic child or Autistic person. Many Autistic people prefer this identity-first language because autism is part of who they are. Some prefer person on the autism spectrum, or another description. Each person's preference matters.

Follow your child's lead wherever possible, and be open to their preferences changing. You may still be finding words that feel comfortable in your family. There's no test on terminology today. Our purpose is to speak respectfully and to listen to how people describe themselves.
segments.source_note: Parents and Carers - Primary, Session 1, slide 9; matching slide PDF page 9; updated PPTX speaker notes (28 September 2026). Authored audience-facing delivery, with optional participation and no invented participant responses.

segments.spoken_text:
Bring your child to mind. What are three things you love or value about them? It might be their humour, an interest they know so much about, the way they connect with someone, or a small moment of joy.

Write those things on page four. For this moment, put the list of challenges to one side and notice who they are. If this is a hard season, one small moment from the past week is enough. Start privately, then share one thing with your table if you wish. Allow four minutes for this reflection and any sharing. Pause the video now, then resume when you are ready to come back.
segments.screen_cue: Allow 4 minutes for reflection and optional sharing. Pause the video, then resume for the debrief.
segments.source_note: Parents and Carers - Primary, Session 1, slide 10; matching slide PDF page 10; updated PPTX speaker notes (28 September 2026). PC Primary - Workbook PDF page 4. Authored audience-facing delivery, with optional participation and no invented participant responses.

segments.spoken_text: Keep that page handy. Those strengths and joys belong in every conversation we have today, including conversations about support. We'll come back to them at the end, when you choose a strength to name to your child.
segments.source_note: Parents and Carers - Primary, Session 1, slide 10; matching slide PDF page 10; updated PPTX speaker notes (28 September 2026). PC Primary - Workbook PDF page 4. Authored audience-facing delivery, with optional participation and no invented participant responses.

segments.spoken_text:
You know your child in ways that nobody else does. You know the familiar routines, the tiny changes, and what a good moment looks like in your family. That knowledge matters here.

We bring information about neurodiversity-affirming practice to put alongside your experience. As we talk it through, you can ask what fits, what doesn't, and what you still want to understand. You don't have to leave with someone else's version of family life. We are looking for ideas you can consider with your own child.
segments.source_note: Parents and Carers - Primary, Session 1, slide 11; matching slide PDF page 11; updated PPTX speaker notes (28 September 2026). Authored audience-facing delivery, with optional participation and no invented participant responses.

segments.spoken_text:
We're going to hear directly from Autistic young people. Listen to their accounts on their own terms. Each speaker offers their own experience. We don't need to compare them with your child or ask one person to represent everyone.

Notice what stays with you, and what it makes you curious to understand more deeply. Let's listen.
segments.source_note: Parents and Carers - Primary, Session 1, slide 12; matching slide PDF page 12; updated PPTX speaker notes (28 September 2026). Authored audience-facing delivery, with optional participation and no invented participant responses.

segments.spoken_text: Take a quiet moment with what you've just heard.
segments.source_note: Parents and Carers - Primary, Session 1, slide 12; matching slide PDF page 12; updated PPTX speaker notes (28 September 2026). Authored audience-facing delivery, with optional participation and no invented participant responses.

segments.spoken_text:
On page four, return to the young people's voices. What did you notice? What stayed with you? And what would you like to understand more deeply about your own child?

Begin with a little private writing. If you share, stay close to what the speakers actually said. It's fine to feel moved, uncertain, or to have a question without an answer. You can talk with someone nearby or keep this reflection to yourself. Pause the video now.
segments.screen_cue: Allow 3 minutes for reflection and optional sharing. Pause the video, then resume for the debrief.
segments.source_note: Parents and Carers - Primary, Session 1, slide 13; matching slide PDF page 13; updated PPTX speaker notes (28 September 2026). PC Primary - Workbook PDF page 4. Authored audience-facing delivery, with optional participation and no invented participant responses.

segments.spoken_text: As we come back, keep one question in mind. Sensory experience, thinking and communication will give us ways to explore it. A question that stays open can be useful. We can listen carefully without assuming we already know what an experience means for someone else.
segments.source_note: Parents and Carers - Primary, Session 1, slide 13; matching slide PDF page 13; updated PPTX speaker notes (28 September 2026). PC Primary - Workbook PDF page 4. Authored audience-facing delivery, with optional participation and no invented participant responses.

segments.spoken_text:
Neurodiversity means the diversity of human brains and minds. It includes everyone. Neurotypical and neurodivergent describe patterns within that wider picture, and autism is one expression of it.

These words help us talk about differences in experience and processing. They don't tell us everything about a particular person. As we explore common patterns today, keep asking how they do, or don't, connect with the child you know. Each child remains an individual.
segments.source_note: Parents and Carers - Primary, Session 1, slide 14; matching slide PDF page 14; updated PPTX speaker notes (28 September 2026). Authored audience-facing delivery, with optional participation and no invented participant responses.

segments.spoken_text:
A neurodiversity-affirming approach recognises different ways of knowing, doing, being and belonging. People think and learn in different ways. Everyone has strengths, and everyone can experience challenges.

Take the things you wrote about your child earlier. Their interests, enjoyment and way of connecting are part of the picture when we think about support. We can take difficulties seriously while valuing who they are. That means asking what the surroundings, routines and support need to look like so your child can participate comfortably and authentically. A hard day doesn't cancel out a strength, and recognising a strength doesn't make a hard day disappear.
segments.source_note: Parents and Carers - Primary, Session 1, slide 15; matching slide PDF page 15; updated PPTX speaker notes (28 September 2026). Authored audience-facing delivery, with optional participation and no invented participant responses.

segments.spoken_text:
Autism is one part of a person's identity. Culture, language, gender, age, disability, faith and family circumstances can overlap and shape opportunities, barriers and experiences. That's the idea of intersectionality.

The words on this slide are prompts to widen our understanding. You don't need to share personal identity information here. For your child, useful support takes account of the whole person and the family context. We can stay curious about parts of their experience we haven't yet understood.
segments.source_note: Parents and Carers - Primary, Session 1, slide 16; matching slide PDF page 16; updated PPTX speaker notes (28 September 2026). Authored audience-facing delivery, with optional participation and no invented participant responses.

segments.spoken_text:
Capacity can change, sometimes within the same day. Something your child managed on a quiet Saturday might be much harder after a full Monday at school. The child is the same, but the demands, sensory load and available energy may be different.

The phrase dynamic disability helps us keep that changing experience in view. When something becomes difficult, ask what else is going on and what support fits now. Yesterday's capacity doesn't tell us exactly what is available today. We'll come back to this in more detail when we talk about daily energy.
segments.source_note: Parents and Carers - Primary, Session 1, slide 17; matching slide PDF page 17; updated PPTX speaker notes (28 September 2026). Authored audience-facing delivery, with optional participation and no invented participant responses.

segments.spoken_text:
Before we finish this first session, let's look at your rights at school. The Disability Discrimination Act of nineteen ninety-two makes it unlawful to treat someone unfairly because of disability, including in education. The Disability Standards for Education were introduced in two thousand and five. These standards set out schools' responsibilities for access and participation.

The school must consult your child, or you on their behalf, about reasonable adjustments so they can take part on the same basis as students without disability. That consultation can include your child directly, you as their parent or carer, or both.

Here are three useful questions to keep: How will we be consulted? What adjustments are in place? How and when will they be reviewed?

This is general information, rather than advice about an individual legal situation. The Department of Education has plain-language guides for families. We'll return to consultation, support pathways and preparing for a conversation with school in Session Five. Knowing your rights gives you a useful starting point for that partnership.
segments.source_note: Parents and Carers - Primary, Session 1, slide 18; matching slide PDF page 18; updated PPTX speaker notes (28 September 2026). Authored audience-facing delivery, with optional participation and no invented participant responses.

segments.spoken_text:
Let's hold on to joy and flourishing as we move forward. Connection, belonging and small moments of enjoyment matter. Every family is different, and understanding what helps can take time.

Doing something differently is fine when it helps your family. A quieter outing, a familiar shared activity or a small success can matter just as much as a bigger milestone. In our next session, we'll begin with how the world arrives through the senses, and then explore attention and thinking. Keep your child's strengths alongside your questions.
segments.source_note: Parents and Carers - Primary, Session 1, slide 19; matching slide PDF page 19; updated PPTX speaker notes (28 September 2026). Authored audience-facing delivery, with optional participation and no invented participant responses.
